title: Warning: The Orgs Who Vet EdTech Safety Are Funded By the Companies They Are Vetting
author: Laura Derrendinger
summary: Laura Derrendinger exposes a structural conflict of interest at the heart of EdTech safety vetting: the organizations charged with evaluating whether digital tools are safe for children are funded by the very companies whose products they assess. The article opens with Vermont's 250th Independence Day as a prompt for declaring schools independent of Big Tech and builds a detailed case that Google and Apple have systematically embedded their products in classrooms through direct funding of the nonprofit vetting infrastructure. Derrendinger cites internal Google documents showing deliberate Chromebook placement in schools as a customer-building strategy targeting children while young, and a March 2026 California jury verdict finding Meta and Google liable for harming children. Vermont Coalition for Independence, Reconnection and Liberation — which Derrendinger co-leads — advanced two legislative priorities: the right to opt out of electronic devices in school, and independent funding for safety vetting organizations. The article makes a clear structural argument: no organization can simultaneously receive funding from EdTech companies and hold independent authority to certify those companies' products as safe for children.
points: The safety vetting conflict is structural: organizations that certify EdTech products as child-safe receive funding from the companies whose products they certify — an incentive structure incompatible with independent evaluation by design.

Internal Google documents confirm that Chromebook placement in schools was a deliberate customer-building strategy: capturing children as users before they have the cognitive development to evaluate commercial influence was an explicit goal, not a side effect.

A March 2026 California jury verdict holding Meta and Google liable for harming children establishes legal precedent that corporate accountability for EdTech harms is enforceable rather than merely theoretical.

Most EdTech currently deployed in schools has not demonstrated learning gains over non-digital alternatives; the standard for adoption should be independent evidence of benefit, not vendor claims or certifications from vendor-funded bodies.

The structural corrective requires separating vetting authority from commercial funding: safety certification organizations must be funded by governments or independent foundations, not by the industry they are charged with evaluating.
quotes: Note from Emily: Laura is one of my oldest friends and allies in the fight against Big Tech and EdTech. We first met in Washington D.C. in 2019, at the first gathering of Fairplay’s Screens-in-Schools working group. Laura is a fierce advocate and I am honored to know her.
This commentary is by Laura Derrendinger, who co-leads the Vermont Coalition for Independence, Reconnection and Liberation [ ].

In March, a jury in California found Meta and Google, which owns YouTube, liable for harming children. An investigation in The New York Times [ ] exposed how both companies planned to capture students’ attention [ ] at school. Yet we’ve allowed Google’s products to become standard issue in nearly all Vermont schoolchildren’s hands.

Vermont students should be free from being targeted by marketing in the classroom. We support digital tools when independent research shows learning gains over nondigital alternatives. Most of what’s in Vermont classrooms today doesn’t meet that bar.

In pushing for that independent verification, testimony from the Agency of Education before the Vermont House Commerce Committee stated that “in the educational technology space, Common Sense Media and the International Society for Technology in Education (ISTE) are trusted sources of information.” [ ]

It’s the same logic as expecting Marlboro to advise on tobacco safety, or Budweiser to teach kids about underage drinking — yet the American Academy of Pediatrics directs parents to Snapchat and Instagram for guidance on keeping kids safe on social media.
